title: The Evil God Hypothesis
rootClaim: The hypothesis that the universe was created by an all-powerful, all-knowing, and supreme evil deity is as philosophically plausible as classical monotheism.

branches.text: Stephen Law's Symmetry Argument: Any theological defense used to explain away evil in a good God's world can be mirrored to explain away good in an evil God's world.

children.text: Reverse Free Will Defense: An Evil God granted humans free will so that they could freely choose to commit horrific evil and cause genuine suffering.
Asymmetry of Natural World: Natural beauty, love, joy, and selfless altruism exist in vast quantities, which an all-powerful Evil God would have no reason to tolerate.
Reverse Soul-Making Theodicy: An Evil God permits instances of genuine love and virtue solely as contrast mechanisms to make ultimate suffering and betrayal more excruciating.
Gratuitous Goodness Paradox: Infinite innocent happiness (e.g., newborn animals playing in uninhabited regions) exists without any sentient observers to experience contrast suffering.
Problem of Good: The existence of profound natural and moral virtue is just as problematic for an Evil God as the Problem of Evil is for a Good God.

branches.text: Classical Meta-ethics: Good is ontological reality while Evil is merely a privation of Good (Privatio Boni), destroying theoretical symmetry.

children.text: Augustinian Privation Theory: Evil cannot exist independently as a substance; it is merely the corruption or absence of good, so a supreme entity must be fundamentally Good.
Privation Asymmetry Fallacy: Good can be symmetrically redefined as the privation of pure malice, proving Privatio Boni is a linguistic convention rather than an objective metaphysical truth.
Ontological Argument Asymmetry: Maximal greatness inherently includes moral perfection (goodness); a maximally evil entity is self-contradictory and metaphysically limited.

definitions.description: A philosophical thought experiment asserting that an omnipotent, omniscient, and malevolent deity created the universe.
The philosophical doctrine defining evil not as an active force, but as the privation or absence of good.
An attempt to reconcile the existence of good (love, beauty, joy) with the existence of a malevolent God.
Stephen Law's argument that the theoretical moves to defend traditional monotheism against the Problem of Evil can be mirrored identically to defend an Evil God against the Problem of Good.
